questions.stem: Food security exists when:
options: food is available in supermarkets, whether or not every household can afford to buy it
all people at all times have access to enough safe, nutritious food for an active, healthy life
a country grows all of the food that its population eats, without relying on any food imports
farmers produce enough food each year to export a surplus to other countries at a profit
questions.explanation: Food security requires that food is available, that people can access and afford it, that it is used to give good nutrition, and that this is stable over time. A country can be food secure while importing food, and food on shelves is not enough if households cannot afford it.

questions.stem: A region produces plenty of grain, but many low-income households cannot afford enough to eat after prices rise sharply. Which aspect of food security is failing?
options: Productivity
Access
Availability
Utilisation
questions.explanation: Availability concerns whether enough food exists, and here it does. Access concerns whether people can obtain it, physically and economically, and rising prices have put food out of reach of poorer households.

questions.stem: Which dimension of food security concerns people having adequate food at all times, including through shocks such as droughts, cyclones and price spikes?
options: Utilisation
Stability
Availability
Access
questions.explanation: Stability means that availability, access and utilisation hold up over time rather than only in good years. Availability is whether enough food is produced or supplied, access is whether people can obtain it, and utilisation is how well the body uses the food eaten.

questions.stem: Which is an environmental challenge to food production rather than an economic or social one?
options: Low household incomes limiting the food people can buy
Trade restrictions limiting the import of staple foods
Soil degradation by erosion, salinity and acidification
Rising fuel prices increasing the cost of food transport
questions.explanation: Erosion, dryland salinity and soil acidification reduce the land's capacity to grow crops, which is an environmental constraint. Fuel prices, household income and trade rules are economic or political factors that affect access rather than the land itself.

questions.stem: Urban growth on the fringe of Melbourne is replacing fertile market gardens with housing. How does this threaten regional food security?
options: It improves soil fertility, because houses and roads protect the soil from erosion
It has no long-term effect, because farmland can always be recreated in another place
It removes productive land close to a large population, raising transport needs and costs
It increases the amount of farmland available, which lowers food prices for households
questions.explanation: Peri-urban farmland near cities is often fertile and supplies fresh food with short transport distances. Once built over it is effectively lost, so food must be grown further away. Equally fertile land with water is not always available elsewhere.

questions.stem: Which factor is a major cause of food loss after harvest in many developing regions?
options: Overuse of refrigerated transport that freezes produce in transit
Selective breeding that makes crops ripen before they can be harvested
Poor storage that allows pests, moisture and mould to spoil crops
Excess use of drip irrigation that floods crops before they are picked
questions.explanation: Without dry, sealed storage and cold chains, much grain and produce is lost to insects, rodents, damp and decay before it reaches consumers. Drip irrigation applies small amounts of water to roots and does not flood crops.

questions.stem: Global food production is sufficient to feed the world's population, yet hundreds of millions of people remain undernourished. What does this most strongly suggest?
options: Food insecurity is driven largely by unequal access, poverty, conflict and waste
Food insecurity is driven largely by too little food being grown worldwide
Food insecurity will be solved automatically by increasing global crop yields
Food insecurity affects only countries that import most of their food supply
questions.explanation: If enough food is produced overall but many still go hungry, the problem lies in distribution and access: poverty, conflict, poor infrastructure and losses along the supply chain. Raising yields alone does not ensure that food reaches those who cannot afford it.

questions.stem: Which practice is permitted in conventional monoculture but not in certified organic farming?
options: Adding composted manure to improve soil fertility
Releasing predatory insects to control crop pests
Spraying synthetic herbicides to control weeds
Rotating crops to break pest and disease cycles
questions.explanation: Certified organic systems exclude synthetic fertilisers, herbicides and pesticides. Crop rotation, compost and biological pest control are all used in organic farming, and some conventional farmers use them too.

questions.stem: What feature do conventional monoculture and organic monoculture systems share?
options: Synthetic pesticides are used to control insects
Crops are grown without any added nutrients
Several crop species are grown in the same rows
A single crop species is grown over a large area
questions.explanation: A monoculture is a single crop grown over a large area, whether managed conventionally or organically. Both therefore have low crop diversity and can be vulnerable to pests that specialise on that crop.

questions.stem: Compared with produce from a conventional monoculture, produce from an organic monoculture is most likely to:
options: be grown with more synthetic fertiliser, giving larger produce
carry fewer synthetic pesticide residues, but cost more to buy
carry more synthetic pesticide residues, but cost less to buy
be identical in every way, apart from the label it carries
questions.explanation: Because synthetic pesticides are not used, organic produce generally carries fewer of their residues. Organic production usually involves more labour and lower or less consistent yields, which tends to raise prices.

questions.stem: Why is an organic farmer more likely than a conventional farmer to include legumes such as clover in a crop rotation?
options: Legumes host nitrogen-fixing bacteria, replacing synthetic nitrogen fertiliser
Legumes release herbicides from their roots, replacing synthetic weed sprays
Legumes absorb pesticide residues, so the soil can be certified as organic
Legumes need no water at all, so they reduce the farm's irrigation requirements
questions.explanation: Rhizobium bacteria in legume root nodules fix atmospheric nitrogen, which enriches the soil for the following crop. Organic farmers cannot use synthetic nitrogen fertiliser, so legumes are a key nitrogen source.

questions.stem: A conventional and an organic wheat farm are compared. The conventional farm has higher yield per hectare; the organic farm has more earthworms and soil organic matter. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The two systems are identical, because both are monocultures of the same wheat crop
Each system has trade-offs: one gives more food per hectare, the other better soil health
The organic farm is better in every way, because soil health always matters more than yield
The conventional farm is better in every way, because higher yield always means more sustainable
questions.explanation: The data show an advantage for each system on a different measure, so neither is better on every criterion. Which matters more depends on the priorities being weighed, such as food supply now against long-term soil fertility.

questions.stem: A pest beetle that feeds only on canola spreads rapidly through a district where thousands of hectares are planted to canola. Which feature of monoculture explains the rapid spread?
options: A low density of host plants, so beetles must travel further
A large, continuous supply of the pest's only food plant
A wide variety of food plants for the pest to choose from
A high number of natural predators living among the crops
questions.explanation: Large areas of one crop give a specialist pest abundant, connected food, so its population can grow and spread quickly. Diverse plantings and habitat for predators, which monocultures lack, tend to slow pest outbreaks.

questions.stem: A government funds a program that trains farmers in drought-tolerant crop varieties and soil-moisture conservation. In terms of change, this is best described as:
options: an enabler that removes the need for any irrigation
an enabler that builds farmers' knowledge and capacity
a barrier that restricts the crops farmers may grow
a barrier that raises the cost of food for all consumers
questions.explanation: Education and extension programs enable change by giving farmers the knowledge to adapt their practices. They do not restrict choices, and drought-tolerant varieties reduce but do not remove the need for water.

questions.stem: In a region, farmers could grow more food, but there are no sealed roads to markets and no cold storage. These are best classified as:
options: organisational enablers of food security
biological barriers to food security
structural barriers to food security
political enablers of food security
questions.explanation: Infrastructure such as roads, storage and markets is structural: without it, food spoils or cannot reach buyers. These factors limit, rather than enable, food security, and they are not biological constraints on growing the crops.

questions.stem: A country has fertile land, but a long civil conflict has displaced farmers and blocked aid convoys. Which option would be least effective at improving food security while the conflict continues?
options: Negotiating safe corridors so that food aid can reach civilians
Distributing food directly to camps for displaced families
Airdropping food to towns that convoys cannot reach
Introducing high-yield crop varieties to the abandoned farmland
questions.explanation: Better crop varieties cannot raise production on land that farmers have been forced to leave, so the barrier is political rather than agricultural. Measures that restore access to food, such as safe corridors and direct distribution, address the actual barrier.

questions.stem: Small farmers in a district form a cooperative that pools their harvests, shares storage and negotiates better prices with buyers. This is best described as:
options: an organisational barrier to food security
a political barrier to food security
a structural barrier to food security
an organisational enabler of food security
questions.explanation: A cooperative is a way of organising producers so they can share costs, reduce losses in storage and gain bargaining power, which helps food security. It removes obstacles rather than creating them, so it is an enabler, not a barrier.

questions.stem: A city food-rescue organisation collects surplus food from supermarkets and delivers it to charities. Which food security challenge does it mainly address?
options: Water scarcity in the irrigation districts supplying food
Loss of farmland to urban growth on the edge of the city
Food waste and access to food for people on low incomes
Soil degradation on the farms that grow the city's food
questions.explanation: Food rescue redirects edible food that would otherwise be wasted to people who struggle to afford enough, improving access. It does nothing about the land and water used to produce the food in the first place.

questions.stem: An ecological footprint measures:
options: the amount of carbon dioxide released by a person's car and household electricity use each year
the number of plant and animal species lost when a region is cleared for farming or housing
the area of productive land and water needed to supply a population's resources and absorb its wastes
the total land area within a country's borders, including deserts, ice and other unproductive land
questions.explanation: Ecological footprint analysis converts consumption of food, materials and energy, and the absorption of carbon dioxide, into the area of biologically productive land and sea needed. Carbon emissions are one part of the footprint, not the whole of it.

questions.stem: Ecological footprints are usually expressed in global hectares. A global hectare is:
options: the average area of land owned by one person across the whole world
a hectare of land measured by satellite rather than by ground survey
a hectare of land or water with world-average biological productivity
a hectare of the most productive farmland found anywhere in the world
questions.explanation: Using a standard unit of world-average productivity allows footprints of different countries, people and products to be compared, even though real land varies greatly in how much it can produce.

questions.stem: Suppose Earth's biocapacity is 1.5 global hectares per person. A country's ecological footprint is 6.0 global hectares per person. How many Earths would be needed if everyone lived like this country's average resident?
questions.explanation: 6.0 ÷ 1.5 = 4 Earths. Multiplying 6.0 by 1.5 gives 9, subtracting gives the shortfall per person of 4.5 global hectares, and 1.5 ÷ 6.0 inverts the ratio.

questions.stem: A region's ecological footprint is larger than its biocapacity. This means the region is:
options: using its resources efficiently, because a large footprint means high productivity
achieving intragenerational equity, because its residents consume more than average
running an ecological deficit, depending on imports or depleting its own resources
running an ecological reserve, with spare capacity it could export to other regions
questions.explanation: When demand exceeds the region's own biological capacity, the gap is met by importing resources, overusing local stocks or releasing more carbon dioxide than can be absorbed. A reserve exists only when biocapacity exceeds the footprint.

questions.stem: Average ecological footprints per person are several times larger in some countries than in others. Which sustainability principle does this comparison mainly highlight?
options: Intragenerational equity
Intergenerational equity
The precautionary principle
The polluter-pays principle
questions.explanation: Intragenerational equity is fairness in the use of resources among people alive today, so large differences in footprint between countries are an equity issue within one generation. Intergenerational equity concerns fairness between present and future generations.

questions.stem: Which is a limitation of ecological footprint analysis?
options: It cannot compare footprints because each country uses a different unit of area
It measures only food consumption, so it ignores energy use and carbon dioxide
It can be calculated only for whole countries, not individuals or businesses
It does not fully account for toxic pollution, biodiversity loss or water quality
questions.explanation: The footprint measures land area for resources and carbon absorption, but impacts such as toxic chemicals, species loss and polluted water are not well captured by an area. It uses a common unit, the global hectare, and can be calculated for individuals, businesses and products.

questions.stem: A household lowers its ecological footprint by switching from beef to legumes for most of its protein. How does this relate to the principle of efficient use of resources?
options: The same land is needed, but the protein is shared more fairly between countries
No resources are saved, because all sources of protein have identical footprints
Less land, water and energy are needed to produce the same amount of protein
More land, water and energy are needed, but the protein is of higher quality
questions.explanation: Cattle convert only a small fraction of the plant matter they eat into meat, so producing beef protein requires far more land and water than producing legume protein directly. Getting the same benefit from fewer resources is efficient resource use.

questions.stem: Why does beef generally have a much larger ecological footprint per kilogram than wheat?
options: Cattle are one trophic level higher, so most energy in their feed is lost before it becomes meat
Wheat is grown only on irrigated land, while cattle graze only on land that receives no rain
Beef is always imported from overseas, while wheat is always eaten close to where it is grown
Beef contains more water than wheat, so the water stored in the meat adds to its footprint
questions.explanation: Cattle are primary consumers, and only about 10% of the energy in the pasture or grain they eat ends up in their bodies, so much more land is needed per kilogram of food. Most Australian beef and wheat are produced domestically, so imports are not the reason.

questions.stem: Tomatoes grown in a heated glasshouse nearby are compared with field-grown tomatoes transported 500 km. Which conclusion about their footprints is most accurate?
options: Both must have identical footprints, because the tomatoes are the same variety
The local tomatoes can have the larger footprint, because heating can outweigh transport
The local tomatoes must have the smaller footprint, because food miles decide the total
The transported tomatoes must have the smaller footprint, because field crops need no inputs
questions.explanation: Food miles are only one part of a product's footprint. Energy used in production, such as heating a glasshouse, can exceed the energy used in transport, so a full assessment of the whole life cycle is needed. Field crops still need water, fertiliser and fuel.

questions.stem: The total volume of fresh water used to produce a product, such as a kilogram of rice, is called its:
options: ecological footprint
biocapacity
catchment yield
water footprint
questions.explanation: A water footprint, also called virtual or embedded water, counts the water used at every stage of production. The ecological footprint measures productive area, not volume of water.

questions.stem: A café calculates the ecological footprint of its coffee and finds that most of it comes from the milk rather than the beans. What is the most useful action this analysis supports?
options: Ignoring the result, since a café's footprint cannot be calculated
Using smaller cups only, since the footprint depends on cup size alone
Offering and promoting plant-based milk, since milk is the largest contributor
Changing coffee bean suppliers, since beans are the largest contributor
questions.explanation: Footprint analysis is most useful when it identifies the largest contributors, so effort can be targeted where it has the biggest effect. Here that is dairy, so reducing milk use or offering alternatives will lower the footprint more than changing beans.

questions.stem: Which irrigation method usually has the highest water-use efficiency?
options: Overhead sprinklers run in the heat of the day
Furrow irrigation along unlined channels
Drip irrigation delivering water to the roots
Flood irrigation of the whole paddock
questions.explanation: Drip irrigation places small amounts of water at the root zone, so little is lost to evaporation, run-off or deep drainage. Sprinklers in hot weather lose much water to evaporation, and unlined channels lose it to seepage.

questions.stem: Which is a demand-side option for improving urban water security, rather than a supply-side option?
options: Installing water-efficient showerheads and appliances
Building a large seawater desalination plant on the coast
Constructing a new dam on a river
Pumping more groundwater from aquifers
questions.explanation: Demand-side options reduce the amount of water people use, such as efficient fittings, restrictions and pricing. Desalination, dams and groundwater pumping all increase the supply of water rather than reducing demand.

questions.stem: Replacing open, earthen irrigation channels with pipes improves water-use efficiency mainly by:
options: reducing losses to seepage and evaporation on the way to farms
increasing the amount of rain that falls on the irrigation district
raising the salinity of the water so crops need less of it
allowing water to flow uphill without any pumping energy
questions.explanation: Open channels lose water by seeping into the soil and evaporating from the surface. Pipes deliver more of the water taken from rivers to the crops, so less needs to be diverted for the same yield.

questions.stem: A farmer spreads straw mulch around fruit trees. How does this reduce water demand?
options: It shades the soil, reducing evaporation from the surface
It absorbs water from the trees, reducing transpiration
It raises the soil temperature, speeding up root growth
It seals the soil, so no rain can reach the tree roots
questions.explanation: Mulch covers and shades the soil, keeping it cooler and slowing evaporation, so more water stays in the root zone. Organic mulch lets rain through to the soil rather than sealing it.

questions.stem: A household of four uses 720 litres of water per day. After installing efficient fittings and a rainwater tank for the toilet, mains use falls to 540 litres per day. What is the percentage reduction?
questions.explanation: The reduction is 720 − 540 = 180 L, and 180 ÷ 720 × 100 = 25%. Dividing 180 by the new value of 540 gives 33%, which uses the wrong base for percentage change.

questions.stem: Treated wastewater from a sewage plant is further treated to a high standard and piped to farms and parks for irrigation. How does this help water security?
options: It reduces the water plants need, because recycled water contains less salt
It reduces demand on drinking water supplies by substituting a recycled source
It increases rainfall in the catchment by returning water to the atmosphere
It improves drinking water quality by mixing recycled water into the reservoirs
questions.explanation: Using recycled water where drinking-quality water is not needed frees up potable supplies for households. It does not change rainfall, and recycled water often contains more salt, not less, which must be managed.

questions.stem: Soil moisture sensors show that the root zone of a vineyard stays moist for four days after watering. The grower had been irrigating every two days. What is the best change?
options: Irrigate at midday instead, which lets the sun warm the water before it reaches roots
Irrigate with more water each time, which flushes the moisture sensors and roots clean
Irrigate when sensors show the soil drying, which reduces water lost to deep drainage
Irrigate every day, which keeps the soil wetter and so improves water-use efficiency
questions.explanation: Watering only when the soil is drying matches irrigation to what the vines actually use, so less water drains below the roots or is wasted. Midday watering increases evaporation losses rather than reducing them.

questions.stem: A wet soil sample has a mass of 50.0 g. After drying in an oven at 105 °C, its mass is 40.0 g. What is its water content as a percentage of the wet mass?
questions.explanation: Water lost is 50.0 − 40.0 = 10.0 g, and 10.0 ÷ 50.0 × 100 = 20% of the wet mass. Dividing by the dry mass of 40.0 g gives 25%, which is a different convention from the one asked for.

questions.stem: Soil from a paddock managed for many years with pasture and compost contains more organic matter than soil from a paddock that has been cultivated every year. Which benefit for food and water security follows?
options: The soil is more easily eroded, so the paddock needs more irrigation water
The soil holds more water and nutrients, so crops cope better with dry spells
The soil drains water faster, so less water is available to the crop's roots
The soil contains fewer microorganisms, so nutrients are recycled more slowly
questions.explanation: Organic matter acts like a sponge and holds nutrients, and it improves soil structure, so more rainfall is stored in the root zone. It also supports a larger, more active community of soil microorganisms, not a smaller one.

questions.stem: During a drought, a city imposes water restrictions and also builds a desalination plant. Which statement best compares the two options?
options: Both options reduce household demand, so the city does not need to change its water prices
Both options depend on rainfall, so neither improves water security during a drought
Restrictions cut demand quickly at low cost; desalination adds reliable supply but uses much energy
Restrictions add reliable supply but use much energy; desalination cuts demand quickly at low cost
questions.explanation: Restrictions reduce use straight away and cost little, but rely on people complying and do not create new water. Desalination provides a supply that does not depend on rainfall, but it is expensive to build and run and uses a large amount of energy.

questions.stem: Water trading in the southern Murray–Darling Basin lets irrigators buy and sell water allocations. How can this improve the efficient use of water?
options: Water can no longer be used for crops, only for the environment
Water tends to move to uses that produce more value per megalitre
Every irrigator receives more water than before the trading began
Rainfall in the Basin increases when more water is bought and sold
questions.explanation: Trading lets water flow from lower-value to higher-value uses, as buyers who gain more from each megalitre can pay more for it. The total water available is still set by rainfall and river flows, not by trading.
